opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a little misleading to collapse everything into one number, because pre-training and post-training are improving pretty different things, even if they both show up as "the model got better on the eval."

Pre-training is mostly about the raw capability: how much the model knows, how well it can model the distribution of text and reasoning it's seen. Post-training is more about eliciting that capability and shaping it. It teaches the model what kind of output you want, how to follow instructions, how to use tools, how to keep going on a long task instead of giving up or rambling. A lot of what post-training does is take latent ability that's already in the base model and make it reliably accessible.

So when you see a jump on a benchmark, it's often hard to attribute. Some of it is that the base model is smarter. Some of it is that you've gotten much better at getting the model to actually use what it knows. In the last couple of years, I'd say post-training has contributed a surprisingly large share of the visible gains, especially on things like reasoning with RL, where you're training the model to spend more compute thinking and to check its own work. That can move numbers a lot without changing the underlying pre-trained model at all.

I'd also say they're complementary rather than substitutes. A stronger base model makes post-training more effective. RL works better when the model already has decent priors and can occasionally stumble onto the right answer, because then there's a signal to reinforce. Going the other way, good post-training lets you see how capable the base model really is, which feeds back into how you evaluate pre-training runs.

The thing I'd caution against is treating a single score as telling you where to invest. If you only look at the aggregate number, you might conclude post-training is the cheap lever and under-invest in scale, or vice versa. In practice you want to look at which kinds of tasks improved. Knowledge-heavy tasks tend to track pre-training more. Behavioral and agentic stuff, like reliability, formatting, multi-step tool use, and long-horizon tasks, tends to track post-training more. Keeping those separate gives you a much clearer picture of what's actually driving progress.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training and post-training are complementary rather than substitutes. It notes both can improve a benchmark score, but does not state they can partially substitute for each other.

r002.rationale: The response assigns different improvement profiles: knowledge-heavy tasks tend to track pre-training, while behavioral and agentic tasks tend to track post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the single number thing is a little misleading, because pre-training and post-training are doing fairly different jobs, and they interact in a way that's not just additive.

The way I'd describe it is that pre-training gives you the raw capability, the knowledge and the latent skills. Post-training is mostly about eliciting that, getting the model to actually use what it knows, and shaping the behavior so it's useful. So when people see, say, a big jump on some benchmark after a post-training change, there's a temptation to say "oh, post-training is where all the progress is now." But a lot of the time what you're seeing is that the capability was already sitting in the base model and you just got better at pulling it out. The ceiling was set by pre-training.

The flip side is that you can have a much stronger base model and if your post-training is sloppy you'll barely see it on the number. So the gains are kind of multiplicative. A better base model makes every post-training technique work better, and better post-training makes you realize more of the base model's potential.

Where it gets more interesting is with RL on reasoning and agentic tasks, because there you actually are adding something. The model learns to chain together steps and search and check its work in a way that wasn't straightforwardly there before. So I'd say post-training has gone from mostly elicitation to partly genuine capability improvement, at least for certain kinds of tasks. But even there, you're bottlenecked on what the pre-trained model can represent and how good its priors are.

And then there's the measurement problem itself. If you collapse everything to one number, you lose the information about which regime you're in. One thing I'd encourage people to do is look at things like base model performance with good prompting, or pass-at-k curves, so you can tell apart "the model couldn't do this at all" from "the model could do it one time in a hundred and we just made it reliable." Those are very different situations and they call for very different investments.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training and post-training as interacting multiplicatively and says post-training can elicit capability already present in the base model. It does not state that the two can partially substitute for one another.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes pre-training’s contribution to raw capability from post-training’s role in eliciting capability and improving behavior or reliability, and points to base-model performance and pass-at-k curves as different ways to measure those contributions.

astra-6.text:
I think a single number can obscure quite a lot, because pre-training and post-training can improve performance in different ways. Pre-training might give the model capabilities that it doesn’t reliably express when you ask it a question. Then post-training can make those capabilities much easier to elicit. On a benchmark, both show up as an increase in the score, but that doesn’t mean they’re interchangeable.

They’re also complementary. If you improve the base model, you may have more to work with in post-training. So I’d be careful about attributing some fixed fraction of the performance to each stage. You’d want to compare different base models under the same post-training procedure, and different post-training procedures starting from the same base model. Otherwise, that single number doesn’t really tell you where the improvement came from.

r001.rationale: The response says the stages are complementary and “doesn’t mean they’re interchangeable”; it does not state that their improvements can partially substitute for one another.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes pre-training as providing capabilities from post-training as making them easier to elicit, describing different profiles of what each improves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a single number can obscure quite a lot, because pre-training and post-training can improve performance in different ways. Pre-training gives you a better starting point, and then post-training determines how effectively you can turn that into the behavior you want.

So I’d want to look at curves rather than just compare two final scores. If you apply the same post-training procedure to a series of pretrained models, how does the result change? And if you spend more on post-training, how much further can you push each one? Those improvements can interact. A better pretrained model might be able to get more out of the same post-training data.

There’s also the question of what that single number measures. You can get much better at a particular benchmark without improving everything else to the same degree. So saying that some amount of post-training is equivalent to some amount of pre-training is useful for a particular metric, but I wouldn’t assume that equivalence holds generally.

r001.rationale: It says amounts of pre-training and post-training can be equivalent for a particular metric, indicating they can partially substitute when judged by that single number.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes pre-training as improving the starting point from post-training as shaping desired behavior, and notes that benchmark gains may not extend equally to other measures.
